claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Its interlamellar boundaries are brittle and prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A controlled post-solidification low-temperature anneal will form or transform a thin, ductile phase at lamellar colony boundaries.
Annealing parameters can be tuned to modify the chemical and crystallographic nature of lamellar interfaces selectively without altering the bulk phases.
The annealing temperature should remain below the bulk recrystallization threshold.
The interfacial phase produced by annealing will enhance interlamellar cohesion and ductility.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion and ductility will reduce stress concentrations and microcrack initiation.
The modified interfaces will permit greater plastic deformation while preserving the load-carrying capacity of the lamellar phases.
Relative to the untreated alloy, annealing will reduce microcrack density.
Relative to the untreated alloy, annealing will improve room-temperature tensile ductility.
Relative to the untreated alloy, annealing will maintain or slightly enhance tensile strength.
The conventional baseline has high strength but limited ductility because of brittle interfacial boundaries.
Excessive annealing may coarsen the bulk lamellae.
Excessive annealing may form deleterious phases.
The intervention is expected to benefit eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar microstructures only within a carefully controlled annealing window.
The intervention may not transfer to alloys with different microstructural architectures.
The exact annealing temperature, duration, and optimal interfacial phase characteristics are unknown.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis promises improved strength and ductility, but the predicted outcome permits strength merely to be maintained. The falsification rule then requires a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility, so a result with improved ductility and unchanged strength is simultaneously predicted and defined as falsifying.
